# Student Performance & Learning Analytics - Final Report

VEDA Technology Data Science Internship - Major Project

## 1. Summary

This project analyses student academic data to find performance patterns, subject-wise strengths and weaknesses, attendance trends, and factors associated with successful outcomes, then builds and evaluates a simple prediction model.

**The data is synthetic.** It was generated by code with a fixed random seed, and relationships such as attendance and study time raising scores were built into it. The report therefore shows that the workflow works and what it produces; it does not report discoveries about real students.

Key results:

- Attendance, study hours and previous score are all positively related to average score (correlations 0.43, 0.45 and 0.54) and are almost independent of each other.
- Students below 60% attendance average 55.2, against 69.8 for those at 90-100%.
- Maths is the weakest subject for the whole group (59.9 average against 67.7 for English).
- A linear regression model explains about 72% of the variation in average score on unseen students, with an average error of 3.4 points.
- The model identifies only 7 of 12 genuinely at-risk students in the test set, so it is not suitable on its own for deciding who needs support.

## 2. Data

The dataset has one row per student with gender, attendance percentage, weekly study hours, previous exam score, parental support level, whether the student attends extra classes, and scores in Maths, Science, English, Social Studies and Computer. The prediction target is the average of the five subject scores. A student is marked **at risk** when that average is below 55.

The raw file contains 612 rows and was made deliberately messy: duplicate rows, categories written in several spellings, missing values, and impossible values.

## 3. Data cleaning

| Step | Rows or values affected |
|---|---|
| Duplicate students removed | 12 |
| Attendance stored as a fraction, rescaled to a percentage | 8 |
| Attendance above 100, set to missing | 6 |
| Negative study hours, set to missing | 5 |
| Subject scores outside 0-100, set to missing | 4 |
| Rows dropped for a missing subject score | 34 |
| Attendance values filled with the median | 36 |
| Study hours values filled with the median | 29 |
| Parental support values filled with the most common level | 18 |

The cleaned dataset has 566 students and no missing values. Rows missing a subject score were dropped instead of filled because the target is built from those scores. Remaining gaps were filled using values from the whole dataset before the train/test split; with at most 6.4% of any column filled the effect is small, but a production pipeline would learn the fill values from training data only.

## 4. Exploratory analysis

Average scores centre on 64.5 (standard deviation 8.8), with 77 students (13.6%) below the at-risk cutoff.

![Distribution of average score](charts/02_average_score_distribution.png)

Parental support shows a clear gap: 61.4 for Low, 64.4 for Medium and 67.9 for High support. Extra classes are associated with 2.6 more points (66.1 against 63.5). Gender shows no meaningful difference (64.4 against 64.6).

![Average score by parental support](charts/03_score_by_parental_support.png)

## 5. Attendance analysis

Average score rises in every attendance band, and the share of at-risk students falls from 48.1% (below 60% attendance) to 5.9% (90-100%).

| Attendance band | Students | Average score | At risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Below 60 | 27 | 55.2 | 48.1% |
| 60-75 | 127 | 60.3 | 22.0% |
| 75-90 | 293 | 65.0 | 9.9% |
| 90-100 | 119 | 69.8 | 5.9% |

![Attendance vs average score](charts/05_attendance_vs_score.png)

The relationship is steeper at low attendance: about 0.82 score points per attendance point below 65%, against 0.34 at or above it. The low group is small (55 students), so that estimate is noisy.

## 6. Subject-wise analysis

English is the strongest subject (67.7) and Maths the weakest (59.9). Maths is the lowest-scoring subject for 54.2% of students and the highest for only 3.5%, so it is a group-wide weakness. Study hours relate most strongly to Maths (r = 0.51) and least to English (r = 0.25).

![Score distribution by subject](charts/06_subject_score_distribution.png)

## 7. Correlation analysis

Previous score (0.54), study hours (0.45) and attendance (0.43) are the three numeric inputs, ranked by correlation with average score. The subjects correlate with each other between 0.70 and 0.77.

![Correlation heatmap](charts/07_correlation_heatmap.png)

## 8. Feature engineering

Parental support, extra classes and gender were encoded numerically. Two features were added because the analysis pointed to them: **LogStudyHours**, since the score gained per extra study hour falls from 2.88 to 0.45 points as study time grows, and **AttendanceShortfall**, the distance below 65% attendance. Subject scores were excluded as features because the target is calculated from them.

![Average score by study hours](charts/08_score_by_study_hours.png)

## 9. Model and evaluation

A linear regression model predicts average score. The data was split 80/20 (452 training students, 114 testing students), and the test students were used only for the final evaluation.

| Model | R-squared (test) | MAE (test) | RMSE (test) | R-squared (5-fold CV) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline (predict the mean) | -0.002 | 6.64 | - | - |
| Linear regression, original features | 0.694 | 3.65 | 4.58 | 0.662 |
| Linear regression, engineered features | 0.721 | 3.43 | 4.38 | 0.689 |

The engineered features improve R-squared by about 0.027 on the test set and 0.027 in cross-validation, a modest but consistent gain. The largest effects, on standardized features, are previous score (4.31), log study hours (3.95) and attendance (2.89).

![Model coefficients](charts/09_model_coefficients.png)

![Predicted vs actual average score](charts/10_predicted_vs_actual.png)

Errors are centred near zero (mean 0.72), with the largest misses about 11.3 points too low and 11.6 too high.

![Prediction errors](charts/11_residuals.png)

**At-risk detection.** Of the 12 at-risk students in the test set the model flagged 7 and missed 5, and it produced 6 false alarms, so 7 of its 13 flags were correct.

## 10. Limitations

- The data is synthetic and its patterns were built in, so findings are demonstrations of method.
- The model is linear and cannot capture interactions between factors.
- The test set is small (114 students), so the figures would shift with a different split.
- Missing values were filled before the split.
- Correlation does not show cause: attendance and study hours may be linked to outcomes through other factors.

## 11. Recommendations

If real data showed the same patterns as this synthetic data:

- Monitor students whose attendance falls below about 65%, where the link to lower scores is steepest and the at-risk share is highest.
- Treat Maths as a group-level issue and review teaching support for it, not only individual interventions.
- Encourage consistent study habits, since the first additional hours of study are associated with the largest gains.
- Do not rely on this model alone to identify students needing help; use it as one input alongside teacher judgement.

## 12. Reproducing the results

Install the packages in `requirements.txt` and run `student_performance_analytics.ipynb` from top to bottom. All data is generated with a fixed random seed, so the same numbers appear on every run.
